Pauline Hanson rules herself of running for Capricornia
Pauline Hanson has ruled herself out of running for the federal seat of Capricornia after Nationals leader Matt Canavan put his hand up.
Incumbent Nationals MP Michelle Landry last month announced she would retire at the next election, opening the door for Canavan to move from the Senate to the House of Representatives.
One Nation party director James Ashby hasn't ruled out contesting the central Queensland seat which includes the towns of Rockhampton and Yeppoon.
Asked this morning in Melbourne whether she would put her hand up for the seat, the One Nation leader said she isn't running.

"Am I running in Capricornia? No I'm not running in Capricornia, so I'll give you a direct answer to that one. What Matt Canavan does is Matt Canavan's choice to do what he wants to do, but it's not my choice to run in Capricornia," Hanson says.
Asked whether Ashby would run for the lower house seat, Hanson wouldn't rule it out.
"Well, we're still over a year out from the election, a year and a half, so I'm not making any decisions for him."
Aerial firefighting fleet will help with evacuations, fodder drops, minister says
Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain has stepped up in Western Sydney to announce a bolstering of the national firefighting fleet.
In May's federal budget, Labor announced $150 million over the next three years to support the National Aerial Firefighting Centre (NAFC).
The NAFC contracts nearly 170 aircraft each year to support states and territories in responding to bushfire emergencies.
McBain says the aircraft will be pre-positioned across the country ahead of the high-risk weather season.
"The important part about our aerial capability now is not only does it deal with fires, but it also deals with evacuations," McBain says.

"It deals with resupply when isolated communities are cut off, deals with animal welfare like emergency fodder drops when it is needed."So we've made sure that this fleet is fit for every event that may, you know, impact Australians lives over this next high risk weather season."

Falling trust in politicians
Trust in federal and state politicians is falling, according to research by McKinnon.

The survey of more than 4,000 people showed 30.5 per cent of respondents trusted federal politicians, with low trust more pronounced among people living in regional areas and those with lower levels of education.
Dishonesty, broken promises and being out of touch were among the key reasons respondents said they had little trust in politicians.
Concerns about declining social cohesion were also reflected in the survey results, with 74 per cent believing Australia was more divided than a year earlier.
About 29 per cent said they did not feel they could freely express their political opinions and ideas.
That feeling was even more strongly held among young men, with about 50 per cent believing they could freely express their political views, down from 73 per cent the previous year.
Minister won't give timeline on Woodside Browse basin project decision
The environment minister hasn't given a timeframe for when he'd approve or reject a Woodside proposal to develop the Browse gas basin off WA's coast.
Earlier this year, the ABC reported that the environment department was expected to deliver its final recommendation report to the minister in mid-to-late 2026.

The project would produce enough gas every year to power 800,000 homes, but any spill could cause an environmental disaster for nearby Scott Reef, a habitat for endangered pygmy blue whales and a nesting site for green turtles.
Murray Watt says the national Environmental Protection Authority needs to assess the level of impact the project would have on the environment.

"Under the former Coalition government, a decision was made at the time that that project was likely to have significant impact on a number of matters of national environmental significance, particularly things like threatened species like pygmy blue whales, green turtles, the Commonwealth Marine Environment," Watt says.
"That's what triggered this all off. That decision that the project was likely to have those significant impacts."
Watt calls on other states to adopt gun buyback
Environment Minister Murray Watt has urged other states to jump on board with the national gun buyback scheme.
The scheme has kicked off in New South Wales today, with the state to split the cost 50-50 with the Commonwealth.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the buyback in the aftermath of the Bondi Beach terrorist attack.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Watt says the federal government doesn't want to "leave holes" in the system.
"In the immediate aftermath of that terrible Bondi incident, we saw the national cabinet meeting where all premiers and all chief ministers signed up to these reforms," Watt says.

"It is disappointing that many of them have, for the moment at least, walked away from those reforms. The more states and territories we can have participating in the gun buyback, the safer Australians would be."We don't want to leave holes in the system where guns can find their way around certain states and find a backdoor into states that are being part of a buyback."

McKenzie warns One Nation not to campaign against Nationals
Bridget McKenzie has urged One Nation not to campaign against her party at the next election, as her leader puts his hand up for a lower house seat.
As widely expected, Nationals Leader Matt Canavan will contest the Queensland seat of Capricornia at the next federal election, if he's pre-selected by the party.
But One Nation's party director James Ashby has left the door open to running in the seat, setting up a potential contest between the two.
"One Nation has made a big song and dance of wanting to fire the liar, wanting to get the prime minister out of The Lodge," McKenzie says.
"There's only one way to remove Albanese as prime minister, and that is to win more seats than the Labor Party in the House of Representatives.

"If One Nation wants to come after the National Party or the Liberal Party, that is one less effort going into getting rid of the Labor Party. I'm interested in getting a bad government out of The Lodge, and I hope that One Nation will join us in that effort."
McKenzie says NSW gun buyback scheme is 'morally wrong'
Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie has urged firearm owners in NSW and the ACT not to rush to hand in their firearms.
A gun buyback scheme for some registered firearms, supported by the federal government, begins in New South Wales today.
It splits the cost of the buyback equally between the commonwealth and New South Wales governments.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the buyback after the Bondi Beach terrorist attack.
But McKenzie, who has opposed the buyback, has told gun owners via ABC Radio National Breakfast not to hand in their firearms.
She says she's not worried if there are more firearms in Australia now than before the Port Arthur massacre if they are lawfully registered.

"I think my advice to law-abiding firearm owners across New South Wales would be 'don't rush to hand your firearms in'. This goes for 12 months and I think we're all hoping the government changes in March in New South Wales and these draconian laws will be no more," McKenzie says.
"It's unjust because you're literally taking people's private property and not paying them due compensation and it's morally wrong."

Minns says everyone should look to cut spending
Chris Minns says he accepts states and territories have a role in reducing spending to help lower inflationary pressures on the economy.
The NSW premier has previously taken aim at the government over its spending after the Reserve Bank's decision to hike interest rates.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, he says he thinks everyone has a responsibility in reducing spending and, according to media reports, the federal government is also looking to cut spending.

"I think everybody needs to do their bit. That includes me and the opposition parties in New South Wales in the immediate run-up to elections. That's when you're at most risk of government spending money that they don't have," Minns says.

"As it relates to the federal government, I understand from media reports that they're likely to do just that and I think everybody's got a responsibility to do what they can to take pressure off the Reserve Bank."
Minns says gun buyback is urgently needed
NSW Premier Chris Minns says the gun buyback scheme is urgent and needed because gun thefts have increased in his state.
Following the Bondi Beach massacre, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced a national government buyback scheme.
The plan was to split the cost of the buyback 50-50 between the Commonwealth and state and territories, but some jurisdictions have resisted.
NSW and the ACT are the only state and territory to have signed up.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Minns said that, while he'd like the scheme to go national, he's happy to go at it alone.

"The truth of the matter is we have more guns in circulation in Australia than before Port Arthur in 1996. This is an urgent and needed reform and I think it will make us safer, not just from mass shootings but also organised crime," Minns says."It's also a leading source of suicide … and that is having access to a handgun in a house. Commonwealth-NSW gun buyback scheme begins today
A joint Commonwealth-New South Wales gun buyback scheme starts today, allowing people to surrender firearms in exchange for money.
NSW and the ACT are the only states and territories to sign up to the scheme, which splits the cost of the buyback 50-50 with the federal government.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the scheme after the Bondi Beach terror attack.
NSW Premier Chris Minns told ABC News Breakfast the buyback was only for registered eligible guns and people would have to make an appointment to surrender firearms.
"It's not cheap but we believe it's worthwhile and hugely important in terms of driving down crime and making our community safer," Minns said.
Plibersek defends tax changes against new housing data
Tanya Plibersek has again defended the federal government's budget tax changes, after new data was released showing the value of homes has dropped.
Cotality data says national house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, with the speed of the decline in home values tracking at the fastest pace seen over the past 40 years.

Its latest national Home Value Index (HVI) was down 1.2 per cent in October and is now 6.7 per cent below its March peak, equivalent to a decline of about $63,400 in the value of the median Australian dwelling.
But speaking to Channel Seven alongside One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, the social services minister says she thinks the changes have made housing more affordable.
"The fact that the growth in house prices is moderated, I think that means that housing will be affordable for my kids and my grandkids one day," Plibersek says.
Plibersek has also been asked about polling showing Treasurer Jim Chalmers has an approval rating of minus 16.
The social services minister has thrown her support behind Chalmers, saying the treasurer is getting the "tough stuff" done.

"The treasurer is at the forefront of that and there's been no reforming treasurer in Australian history that hasn't copped it when they've made big changes and we all support Jim, we all make decisions together," she says.

PM to seek change to UK free trade agreement at CHOGM

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will seek a tightening of rules for British backpackers coming to Australia when he meets his UK counterpart this week at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua.

In what will be his first official bilateral discussion with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Albanese will seek to reverse part of the Morrison-era UK free trade agreement (FTA) that exempts British backpackers from regional and rural work.
The number of British backpacker visas has doubled to almost 80,000 per year since the 2021 decision.
The government has already imposed a lottery system to stem the flow of working holiday-makers and issued a go-slow on processing UK backpacker visas to reduce net overseas migration.
While the FTA is already law, it's understood regional work rules could be reimposed on British working holiday-makers with the consent of the UK government.
